Also, the "Ke" was computed by calling two R functions:

Runique <- nimbleRcall (
  function (x=double (1) ){}, Rfun="unique",
  returnType=double (1))

Rlength <- nimbleRcall (
  function (x=double (1) ){}, Rfun="length",
  returnType=double (1))

Ke <- Rlength(Runique(groupe[1:N]))

Is this the right way to call R functions in nimble?

Thanks a lot for your time.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
hi Chris, a bit of follow-up to Perry's comments.

For a CRP model you should either define taue.mix to have length equal to the maximum number of clusters, which is N, or you could set it to some _fixed_ smaller number, in which case Nimble's MCMC will warn you if the MCMC tries to use more clusters than the fixed number (and you could then bump the number up and try again). Setting to N is safe, but involves overhead/inefficiency in various ways from having the N nodes in the model. We have some discussion of the issue here <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-bnp.html#sec:excrp>.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Hope this email is finding you well. I have been trying to compute the different predictive performance metrics used in Broms et al. (2010) as a model selection criteria in occupancy models using k-fold cross-validation. (Broms, K. M., Hooten, M. B., & Fitzpatrick, R. M. (2016). Model selection and assessment for multi‐species occupancy models. Ecology, 97(7), 1759-1770.)  I think NIMBLE can be a great tool to implement such metrics ina computationally efficient way.

I begin by computing the Brier score based on the (1) detection-non detection data left out in each fold and retained as the validation data, and (2) the unconditional probability of detection (i.e, the probability that a species is present and detected) estimated from the subsamples used in the training data. Similarly, I computed the 0-1 score based on the posterior predictive values and the known-out-of-sample data values.

My first take on this was to use the runCrossValidate() function to compute the  0-1 score but I don't know if a different loss function (e.g. the ones commonly used for logistic regression) could be used such as AUC, Brier score, log-loss, etc. Thus, I  Implemented a 5-fold cross-validation manually by defining a nimble function that plugs in the posterior estimates of each MCMC sample to simulate the response values in each fold and compared them against the true values in the out-of-sample data (or compute the brier score based on the unconditional detection probability). However, I encountered a few problems that hopefully you can help me with.

(1) The results from using the runCrossValidate() function and the manual approach are slightly different and I am not sure if this could be because of the random allocation or because I am specifying something wrong in the runCrossValidate argument (especially with the dimensions). I tried different seeds and the results are still somewhat different.

(2)  the manual approach works when folds are of the same size because I can simply change the data values in a loop without recompiling the model in each fold. I don't think there is a way of avoiding recompiling the model each time when the size between folds is different right? (because the size in the training and test sets are declared as constant in the operational model)

(3) I defined a nimble function for defining the loss function scores and tried to use it in my second nimble function to compute the actual scores after simulating the data set. However, when I try to compile the second function I get an error that says failed to create a shared library. In the meantime, I defined the loss function directly into my second nimble function using simple R operations supported for NIMBLE but it would be great if you could help me to understand what am I doing wrong by implementing a user-defined function within the run argument of another nimble function.

I have attached a reproducible code.

Many thanks,

Jafet

Thanks for the questions.  This sounds interesting.

runCrossValidate has a good bit of room to be generalized one day, so indeed you might run into some limitations.

For using a different loss function, have you tried working with the lossFunction argument (see help(runCrossValidate))?  It can be simply an R function (not necessarily a nimbleFunction).  However you may already be past that point.

I'm not sure what would cause your different results.  Even with different seeds, it seems likely that the exact order of any random number draws is not the same between your code and nimble's code, so I would only expect a statistical match, not exactly matched numbers.  I did not run and study the differences.

You are correct that the model needs to be recompiled for each fold.  There are slicker ways to work around this, but they are not automated in runCrossValidate, and you have already built your own tools.

I did not run all of your code (thanks for providing it simply and clearly), but I did succeed in the three compileNimble calls on lines 200-205, including the clossSampler.  Is this the one that wasn't working for you?  That's what I am guessing from what you described, so I am not sure where there is a reproducible compilation failure.  There have been some bug fixes recently so I can give the generic suggestion to be sure you've updated nimble.  Otherwise can you say more about where there is a reproducible compilation failure in your code?

Best wishes,
Perry

Hi Jessica,

I'll take a try at this, but as you recognize these can be nebulous topics!  See below.

On Wed, May 11, 2022 at 8:05 AM Jessica Burnett <jessicale...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Could someone point me to resources or share insights on the estimated influence of the following topics on speed?
>
> Specific info/resource request topics:
> 1. Impact of number of posterior samples saved on speed (ignoring the compilation times). That is, would removing any or all monitors even make a major dent in speed?

Conceivably.  Sometimes people don't realize how quickly they can fill up tons of memory even on modern machines.  In case it helps, the calculation to do is:
number of monitored dimensions * number of iterations * 8 bytes per double precision number / 2^20 = # of gigabytes your posterior will fill.

If that is really large, it can impact processing speed as the computer spends time during the run with large memory management duties and accesses.

You can use the monitors2, which has its own thinning, thin2, as a way to save fewer samples of some nodes.  Often this is helpful for example for large numbers of latent states  or random effects.

> 2. Impact of performing various calculations for derived qtys on speed

It depends on what the calculations are, but potentially yes.  One thing I would try to avoid if you are in a performance crunch is stochastic predictive nodes.  In some cases, it can work well to get derived quantities after running the MCMC, but the exception is if the derived quantities are functions of many dimensions that return few dimensions, and you don't want to store the many dimensions in order to calculate these later.

Derived quantities may be calculated on every MCMC iteration even if they are only needed to be stored as output on thinning intervals.  It is on the development to-do list to provide a system that would save the unnecessary computation that may be occurring.

>
>
> Vague background:
> We are building an integrated population to estimate bird abundance across a gridded surface. Our model is severely slowed by the following:
> 1. Spacetime generalized additive model (for latent abundance)
> 2. Jointly sampling the GAM coefficients (using AF_slice;  RW_block has inferior mixing speed).

Some ideas for you: RW_block using control parameter "tries = n" where n is a number such as half the number of dimensions.  This will run n repeats of the RW_block sampler, which can work well because each repeat is fast (compared to other methods) but if there is only one try and that is a rejection, then no mixing occurs on that iteration.  (Until recenly the tries argument did not appear in help(samplers), an oversight we fixed.)  AF_slice is indeed costly but can mix well.  It can also work well to break down the full set of GAM coefficients into smaller blocks and sample each smaller block using either RW_block or AF_slice.

> 3. Calculations are vectorized

This helps when all the calculations will always be done together anyway in the structure of the model.  But it hurts if only individual elements would need to be calculated during an MCMC update of a parent parameter.

> 4. No unnecessary calculations
>
> I also read the Turek et al 2021 paper <https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecs2.3385> and I think we've done everything relevant in our model to implement their recommendations.

Fantastic.  This sounds like a really challenging problem you're tackling.  Thanks for the posting.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Oops -- forgot to include note on why I suspect it was, in fact, an Rtools issue:
When attempting to run:
>     Rmodel.comp <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
I receive error:

> Error: Failed to create the shared library. Run 'printErrors()' to see the compilation errors.

Running:
> printErrors()
yields:
> In system(cmd) : 'make' not found

Which suggests and Rtools issue (unless the error is misleading, which I suspect it isn't).

> On Friday, May 13, 2022, Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> > Hi Jessica,
> >
> > I'll take a try at this, but as you recognize these can be nebulous topics!  See below.
> >
> > On Wed, May 11, 2022 at 8:05 AM Jessica Burnett <jessicale...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Could someone point me to resources or share insights on the estimated influence of the following topics on speed?
> > >
> > > Specific info/resource request topics:
> > > 1. Impact of number of posterior samples saved on speed (ignoring the compilation times). That is, would removing any or all monitors even make a major dent in speed?
> >
> > Conceivably.  Sometimes people don't realize how quickly they can fill up tons of memory even on modern machines.  In case it helps, the calculation to do is:
> > number of monitored dimensions * number of iterations * 8 bytes per double precision number / 2^20 = # of gigabytes your posterior will fill.
> >
> > If that is really large, it can impact processing speed as the computer spends time during the run with large memory management duties and accesses.
> >
> > You can use the monitors2, which has its own thinning, thin2, as a way to save fewer samples of some nodes.  Often this is helpful for example for large numbers of latent states  or random effects.
> >
> > > 2. Impact of performing various calculations for derived qtys on speed
> >
> > It depends on what the calculations are, but potentially yes.  One thing I would try to avoid if you are in a performance crunch is stochastic predictive nodes.  In some cases, it can work well to get derived quantities after running the MCMC, but the exception is if the derived quantities are functions of many dimensions that return few dimensions, and you don't want to store the many dimensions in order to calculate these later.
> >
> > Derived quantities may be calculated on every MCMC iteration even if they are only needed to be stored as output on thinning intervals.  It is on the development to-do list to provide a system that would save the unnecessary computation that may be occurring.
> >
> > >
> > >
> > > Vague background:
> > > We are building an integrated population to estimate bird abundance across a gridded surface. Our model is severely slowed by the following:
> > > 1. Spacetime generalized additive model (for latent abundance)
> > > 2. Jointly sampling the GAM coefficients (using AF_slice;  RW_block has inferior mixing speed).
> >
> > Some ideas for you: RW_block using control parameter "tries = n" where n is a number such as half the number of dimensions.  This will run n repeats of the RW_block sampler, which can work well because each repeat is fast (compared to other methods) but if there is only one try and that is a rejection, then no mixing occurs on that iteration.  (Until recenly the tries argument did not appear in help(samplers), an oversight we fixed.)  AF_slice is indeed costly but can mix well.  It can also work well to break down the full set of GAM coefficients into smaller blocks and sample each smaller block using either RW_block or AF_slice.
> >
> > > 3. Calculations are vectorized
> >
> > This helps when all the calculations will always be done together anyway in the structure of the model.  But it hurts if only individual elements would need to be calculated during an MCMC update of a parent parameter.
> >
> > > 4. No unnecessary calculations
> > >
> > > I also read the Turek et al 2021 paper <https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecs2.3385> and I think we've done everything relevant in our model to implement their recommendations.
> >
> > Fantastic.  This sounds like a really challenging problem you're tackling.  Thanks for the posting.
> >
> > -Perry

 C.sim[b,v] ~ dbin( p[year_id[v],b], N[site_id[v], year_id[v], b] )

Nimble is giving me the following warnings, consecutively/simultaneously, for some (but not all!) values of C.sim[b,v] and N[s,t,b], which seem to create an infinite loop such that the model never fits:

"warning: problem initializing stochastic node C.sim[1, 1]: logProb is -Inf."

"Warning: slice sampler reached maximum number of contractions for 'N[1, 1, 1]'. Current parameter value is 59."

I thought it might just be that I need initial values for C.sim, since occasionally that happened with N and I learned on this listserv that could be fixed by adding an init for lambda. But, there's not quite a lambda equivalent for C.sim, and adding an init for C.sim itself has not helped:

inits <- list(
  C.sim = array(1, dim =c(
    n.data$nspecies,
    n.data$nvisits)),
  lambda = array(1, dim =c(
    n.data$nyears,
    n.data$nspecies)),
  N = Nst,
  p = array(0.3, dim = c(
    n.data$nyears,
    n.data$nspecies))
)

Is there a way to solve this? Thanks for any advice! Full code below my name.

Best,
Gates

# ---- Specifying the model ----

n.code <- nimbleCode( {

  # PRIORS
  for(b in 1:nspecies){
    for(t in 1:nyears){

      # Expected count
      lambda[t,b] ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)
      # Detection probability
      p[t,b] ~ dunif(0,1)

    }
  }

  # LIKELIHOOD
  # Ecological model
  for(b in 1:nspecies){
    for(t in 1:nyears){
      for(s in 1:nsites) {

        # Latent site abundance
        N[s,t,b] ~ dpois(lambda[t,b])

      }
    }
  }

  # Observation model
  # Using nested indexing because there is a lot of missing data!
  for(b in 1:nspecies){
    for(v in 1:nvisits){

      # Observed count
      C[b,v] ~ dbin( p[year_id[v],b], N[site_id[v], year_id[v], b] )

    }
  }

  # GOODNESS-OF-FIT
  for(b in 1:nspecies){
    for(v in 1:nvisits){
      # # Commenting out parts that require C.sim
      # # Create new data set under model
      C.sim[b,v] ~ dbin( p[year_id[v],b], N[site_id[v], year_id[v], b] )
      # # Expected datum
      e.count[b,v] <- N[site_id[v], year_id[v], b] * p[year_id[v],b]
      # # Chi-square discrepancy for the actual data
      chi2.actual[b,v] <- pow((C[b,v]-e.count[b,v]),2) / (e.count[b,v]+0.001)
      # # Chi-square discrepancy for the simulated ('perfect') data
      # chi2.sim[b,v] <- pow((C.sim[b,v]-e.count[b,v]),2) / (e.count[b,v]+0.001)
      # # Add small value e to denominator to avoid division by zero
    }
  }

  # # Add up individual chi2 values for overall fit statistic
  fit.actual <- sum(chi2.actual[1:nspecies,1:nvisits]) # Fit statistic for actual data set
  # fit.sim <- sum(chi2.sim[1:nspecies,1:nvisits]) # Fit statistic for a fitting model
  # c.hat <- fit.actual / fit.sim # c-hat estimate
  # bpv <- step(fit.sim-fit.actual) # Bayesian p-value

})

# ---- Defining settings for the model and MCMC ----

inits <- list(
  C.sim = array(1, dim =c(
    n.data$nspecies,
    n.data$nvisits)),
  lambda = array(1, dim =c(
    n.data$nyears,
    n.data$nspecies)),
  N = Nst, # created elsewhere
  p = array(0.3, dim = c(
    n.data$nyears,
    n.data$nspecies))
)

# Parameters monitored
# params <- c("lambda", "p", "fit.actual", "fit.sim", "c.hat", "bpv")
params <- c("lambda", "p")

# MCMC settings
ni <- 25000   ;   nt <- 20   ;   nb <- 5000   ;   nc <- 3

# ---- Prepping and running the MCMC ----

hcm_mod <- nimbleModel(n.code, constants = n.data,
                       check = F, calculate = F)

hcm_mcmc <- buildMCMC(hcm_mod, monitors = params)

hcm_comp0 <- compileNimble(hcm_mod)

hcm_comp <- compileNimble(hcm_mcmc, project = hcm_mod)

hcm_samples <- runMCMC(
  hcm_comp,
  thin = nt,
  nburnin = nb,
  niter = ni,
  nchains = nc,
  inits = inits)

> On Wed, May 11, 2022 at 8:05 AM Jessica Burnett <jessicale...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Could someone point me to resources or share insights on the estimated influence of the following topics on speed?
> >
> > Specific info/resource request topics:
> > 1. Impact of number of posterior samples saved on speed (ignoring the compilation times). That is, would removing any or all monitors even make a major dent in speed?
>
> Conceivably.  Sometimes people don't realize how quickly they can fill up tons of memory even on modern machines.  In case it helps, the calculation to do is:
> number of monitored dimensions * number of iterations * 8 bytes per double precision number / 2^20 = # of gigabytes your posterior will fill.
>
> If that is really large, it can impact processing speed as the computer spends time during the run with large memory management duties and accesses.
>
> You can use the monitors2, which has its own thinning, thin2, as a way to save fewer samples of some nodes.  Often this is helpful for example for large numbers of latent states  or random effects.
>
> > 2. Impact of performing various calculations for derived qtys on speed
>
> It depends on what the calculations are, but potentially yes.  One thing I would try to avoid if you are in a performance crunch is stochastic predictive nodes.  In some cases, it can work well to get derived quantities after running the MCMC, but the exception is if the derived quantities are functions of many dimensions that return few dimensions, and you don't want to store the many dimensions in order to calculate these later.
>
> Derived quantities may be calculated on every MCMC iteration even if they are only needed to be stored as output on thinning intervals.  It is on the development to-do list to provide a system that would save the unnecessary computation that may be occurring.
>
> >
> >
> > Vague background:
> > We are building an integrated population to estimate bird abundance across a gridded surface. Our model is severely slowed by the following:
> > 1. Spacetime generalized additive model (for latent abundance)
> > 2. Jointly sampling the GAM coefficients (using AF_slice;  RW_block has inferior mixing speed).
>
> Some ideas for you: RW_block using control parameter "tries = n" where n is a number such as half the number of dimensions.  This will run n repeats of the RW_block sampler, which can work well because each repeat is fast (compared to other methods) but if there is only one try and that is a rejection, then no mixing occurs on that iteration.  (Until recenly the tries argument did not appear in help(samplers), an oversight we fixed.)  AF_slice is indeed costly but can mix well.  It can also work well to break down the full set of GAM coefficients into smaller blocks and sample each smaller block using either RW_block or AF_slice.
>
> > 3. Calculations are vectorized
>
> This helps when all the calculations will always be done together anyway in the structure of the model.  But it hurts if only individual elements would need to be calculated during an MCMC update of a parent parameter.
>
> > 4. No unnecessary calculations
> >
> > I also read the Turek et al 2021 paper <https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecs2.3385> and I think we've done everything relevant in our model to implement their recommendations.
>
> Fantastic.  This sounds like a really challenging problem you're tackling.  Thanks for the posting.

I'm using nimbe for the first time after using JAGS and coding my own MCMCs. This is such a great middle ground between those two approaches! I'm loving the package and am impressed by the speed!

I'm trying to conduct some posterior predictive checks on a removal model (abundance model) I fit using nimble. The data model is:

y[j,t,i] ~ dbin(N[j,t,i], p[j,t,i])

where y[j,t,i] is the number of animals removed in hunt season j, year t, in site i. N is abundance and p is detection probability, indexed the same. I model p as a function of survey effort and N as a function of landscape and temporal covariates. I don't think the rest of the model structure is relevant here though.

I'm trying to calculate a posterior predictive p-value using deviance (-2* log likelihood) for the data (y) and predicted data points (y.pred). I was able to simulate y.pred using an example posterior prediction nimbleFunction I found in the documentation. I would like to calculate deviance using nimble, and I believe I want nimbleModel$calculate(), but I am am confused about what values this function uses to calculate log probability. I would like to calculate the log probability of both the data and the predictions for each MCMC sample of N and p. I tried a sample (first data point only) using base R and it's incredibly slow (hence wanting to use nimble), but this is what I'm trying to do:

samples <- (MCMC samples obtained via nimble)
ppSamples <- (poseterior predictive samples obtained through simulation)

ind <- numeric(niter)
for(i in 1:niter/2){ #[j,t,i]
#deviance of predictions
  dev.pred <- -2*sum(dbinom(ppSamples[,"y[1, 1, 1]"],
                         samples[i,"N[1, 1, 1]"],
                         samples[i,"p[1, 1, 1]"],log=T))

              samples[i,"N[1, 1, 1]"],
              samples[i,"p[1, 1, 1]"],log=T))
  ind[i] <- dev.pred > dev.y
}
p.val <- mean(ind)

I hope I provided adequate background to address my question, but if not please let me know.

Thanks again,
Abbey

deps <- getDependencies(c('p','N'), self = FALSE)  # this would be in setup code

model$calculate(deps)    # these lines would be in run code
model$getLogProb(c('y','y.pred'))

-chris

 N[1,1] ~ dcat(pinit) # 1st age class
 N[2,1] ~ dcat(pinit) # 2nd age class

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Thanks to the dev team for your work on NIMBLE and everyone here for your contributions to submitted questions - I have learned a ton from monitoring this group! Today I have a question of my own to contribute.

I am working on an integrated population model for a long-lived species. The model itself is relatively simple - m-array likelihood for adult and juvenile survival from capture-mark-resight data, binomial likelihood for productivity, and a normal observation process on population counts. The thing that I think is complicating things is that there is a relatively complex age structure. Individuals can be nearly 40 before recruiting into the breeding population, but most individuals recruit by age 15 or so. I've been experimenting with this model for a few weeks trying to get it to converge in NIMBLE, with no luck. Out of curiosity, I fit the same model in JAGS and I find the results perplexing. While JAGS mixes better, the estimates of the latent abundances especially in the matrix of immature individuals (IM[, , ]) are implausible. In contrast, in NIMBLE many of these nodes mix for a few iterations and then inexplicably stop. However, that may be acceptable as the expected value for many of these nodes is zero. Worryingly, though - many of the total abundances (N.breed.ready, N.recruits, and N.tot.breed) are not mixing at all in NIMBLE. I am writing to see if anyone has any insights into the difference in behavior of JAGS and NIMBLE here and I would love to hear suggestions with regards to how to get this thing to converge. I would prefer to fit this model in NIMBLE so that I can make use of some of the customizability as we hope to add some complexity to the model, if possible.

I have attached a reproducible example of the same model fit in NIMBLE and JAGS, along with the necessary initial values and data objects. I have also attached traceplots of the last 2000 iterations of a 200000 iteration run in both JAGS and NIMBLE. You can see from these traceplots that JAGS and NIMBLE are sampling very different parameter spaces for the latent abundances, which leads to big differences in the estimates of total abundance. I recognize that these models are unconverged, but I would still expect them to be more similar after this many iterations, given the same model. Here is a pesky example of the same node in NIMBLE (not mixing) vs JAGS (mixing, albeit rather poorly). This result is consistent regardless of whether I use initial values or not.

Thanks all for your insights,

Abby Bratt

messages.body_plain:
Hi Abby,

Thanks for this posting.  The code and data worked and were helpful (but I added a call to set.seed for reproducibility).

I think there are a few things going on.  One is your inits$IM is not the same size as Rmodel$IM.  Did you get an obscure message about "R object of different size than NimArrDouble"?  The size mismatch in IM is generating that message.  Unfortunately it means that inits$IM is not being used. (If you didn't get that message, something might be wrong in my trying to reproduce what happened for you.) That particular message isn't very helpful because there are a lot of situations that could trigger it, most of which we hope to catch more helpfully before hitting that message, but it was a real flag that something was wrong.  I'm going to file an issue on GitHub to do more proactive error-trapping of size mismatches when setting inits and see if we can provide more useful error information.

A consequence is that after the first chain, the second chain can end up with invalid initialization and then go into catastrophic mixing, with values that are impossible in the model.  How does this happen?  The first chain doesn't get IM initialized, so the MCMC initializes it by drawing from the prior.  This seems to work in the sense that it runs and no values are invalid.  But the model then gets initialized again for the second chain.  Because inits$IM is not the right size, it is not used and the values in IM in the model remain from the end of the first chain. But other variables do get reset from inits values.  Because you have a lot of dbinom cascades, this can create impossible inits, like the dbinom outcome being larger than the number of trials (size).  Impossible inits in a complicated model structure like this can create unpredictable results.

And I think there is also an issue arising from the model structure.  It looks like there is a single sigma.obs[s, t] value for each y.count[t, s], and each sigma.obs[s,t] has an independent prior.  I think what will happen is that the mixing will find values of Ntot.breed[t]*prop.sites[t,s] that exactly match y.count[t,s] and then sigma.obs[s, t] will end up at effectively 0.  At that point, I think mixing will be very stuck.  Any updates that would change Ntot.breed[t]*prop.sites[t,s] will be rejected because the log prob for y.count[t,s]  will be essentially infinite (like x ~ dnorm(5, sd = 1e-10), with x = 5).  And any updates that would increase sigma.obs[s, t] will be rejected for the same reason.  If this is what's happening it might create a huge multimodality problem because *any* sets of Ntot.breed[t]*prop.sites[t,s]  that match y.count[t,s]  would get locked in, or nearly locked in, in the chains.  Even if you did not monitor sigma.obs, you can check its values in the compiled model after running MCMC: Cmodel$sigma.obs. When I got things running on my system, the Cmodel$sigma.obs were all nearly 0.  For sure it is possible I was not understanding something.

I'm guessing you ran into warnings about maximum number of contractions in the slice sampler(s), because I see you manually changed that.  It is almost always the case that that warning means something is really amiss, not just in need of an adjusted tuning parameter.  In this case it arose basically because once there were invalid values in the model, the sampler could become endlessly confused.

I hope this helps.

Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Keith,

For a non-scalar stochastic node, it can be a bit less obvious what the size of the logProbs object will be.  A non-scalar stochastic node needs only one logProb value.  In this case, response[n,item_index[k,1]:item_index[k,2]] declares stochastic vector nodes.  From item_index, I see the second index for response will be either 1:3, 4:6, or 7:9.  Normally the logProb entry will go in the first available element of an object (logProb_response) the same shape as the random variable but with unneeded extents dropped.  In this case, column 7 of logProb_response is needed for the nodes using columns 7:9 of response, but there is no need for columns 8:9 of logProb_response, so they are dropped.  (There can still be unused space in logProb_response, but that is in the service of some simplicity, but we do drop unneeded space beyond the last needed extent in the logProb, if that makes sense.)

I hope that helps and let me know if it's not clear.

Perry

Dear Keith

I'm not an author of nimble, but perhaps this can help...

In your model, response[n, ] is a vector that holds three realisations of a length 3 mvnorm random variable.

For each element of a given multi-variate (length 3) sub-vector getLogProb returns the same value. e.g.
getLogProb(cmodel,"response[1,1]") # -3.034255
getLogProb(cmodel,"response[1,2]") # -3.034255
getLogProb(cmodel,"response[1,3]") # -3.034255
getLogProb(cmodel,"response[1,4]") # -4.096456
getLogProb(cmodel,"response[1,5]") # -4.096456
getLogProb(cmodel,"response[1,6]") # -4.096456
getLogProb(cmodel,"response[1,7]") # -4.414663
getLogProb(cmodel,"response[1,8]") # -4.414663
getLogProb(cmodel,"response[1,9]") # -4.414663
getLogProb(cmodel)                            # -1372.911

Now let's compare to the values of logProb returned by the MCMC. I use "#" to indicate the output on my machine.

colnames(logProb)[c(1,101,201)]   # "logProb_response[1, 1]" "logProb_response[1, 2]" "logProb_response[1, 3]"
tail(logProb, n=1)    [c(1,101,201)]   # -3.034255  0.000000  0.000000

So we have the same value as above is position 1, and zeros in the following two columns.

colnames(logProb)[300+c(1,101,201)]  # "logProb_response[1, 4]" "logProb_response[1, 5]" "logProb_response[1, 6]"
tail(logProb, n=1)[300+c(1,101,201)]      # -4.096456  0.000000  0.000000

Again, the same value as above is position 1, and zeros in the following two columns.

colnames(logProb)[600+c(1,101,201)]  # "logProb_response[1, 7]" NA                       NA
tail(logProb, n=1)[600+c(1,101,201)]     # -4.414663        NA        NA

Again, same value as above, but here nimble has truncated the two columns of zeros (so the indexing results in NA).

sum(tail(logProb, n=1))              # -1372.86

Close to the above value, presumably computational rounding error explains the difference.

All the best
David
